Westminster Larger Catechism
WEST-min-ster LAR-jer KAT-uh-kiz-um
noun phrase (document)
One of the catechisms produced by the Westminster Assembly (1643-1652). "Larger" distinguishes it from the Westminster Shorter Catechism; both accompany the Westminster Confession of Faith.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Westminster Larger Catechism (1647) is the fuller of the two catechisms produced by the Westminster Assembly, designed for the public exposition of Christian doctrine and for the instruction of those advanced in the faith, while its companion the Shorter Catechism served for the beginner and the child. Together with the Westminster Confession of Faith and the Shorter Catechism, it forms the Westminster Standards, the doctrinal foundation of English-speaking Presbyterianism. Consisting of 196 questions and answers, the Larger Catechism follows the same structure as the Shorter — what man is to believe concerning God, and what duty God requires of man — but in far greater detail. It contains the most extensive confessional exposition of the Ten Commandments in the Reformed tradition, drawing out from each commandment its required duties and forbidden sins with searching thoroughness (so that the seventh commandment, for instance, is shown to forbid not only adultery but every impurity of thought, word, look, and deed). Its treatment of the office and work of Christ, of the sacraments, of the church, and of the means of grace is correspondingly full. While the Shorter Catechism became the universal instrument of basic instruction, the Larger Catechism served preachers, teachers, and serious students as a comprehensive doctrinal and ethical reference. Its exposition of the moral law in particular has shaped Reformed ethics for nearly four centuries, and it remains a subordinate standard in confessional Presbyterian churches and a treasured resource across the broader Reformed world.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The fuller of the two Westminster catechisms (1647), 196 questions for advanced instruction and public exposition; contains the most extensive Reformed confessional treatment of the Ten Commandments; part of the Westminster Standards with the Confession and Shorter Catechism.

WESTMINSTER LARGER CATECHISM, noun phrase. The fuller Westminster Assembly catechism (1647).

196 questions and answers; designed for public exposition and the advanced student.

Companion to the Shorter Catechism (for beginners) and the Westminster Confession; together the Westminster Standards.

Contains the most extensive confessional exposition of the Ten Commandments in the Reformed tradition (required duties and forbidden sins under each).

A subordinate standard in confessional Presbyterian churches; a treasured Reformed resource.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Westminster Larger Catechism is corrupted when its thorough exposition of the law is dismissed as legalism, when it is neglected in favor of the Shorter Catechism alone, or when its searching application of the commandments to thought and motive is softened to accommodate the modern conscience.

expand to see more

Law-as-legalism misreading. The Larger Catechism's exhaustive exposition of the Ten Commandments — drawing from each commandment a wide range of required duties and forbidden sins, reaching to the thoughts and motives of the heart — can be mistaken for legalism, as though it bound the conscience to an oppressive code. The Reformed reading is the opposite: the law searched in this depth drives the sinner to Christ (the law's pedagogical use, Gal 3:24), and serves the believer as the rule of grateful obedience (the law's third use). The Catechism expounds the law so thoroughly precisely to show that no one can be justified by it, and to direct the justified believer in the path of holiness. The thoroughness serves the gospel.

Neglect for the Shorter alone. Most who know the Westminster catechisms know only the Shorter — rightly beloved for its compact, memorizable answers. The Larger Catechism, longer and less often memorized, is correspondingly neglected. Yet it contains treasures the Shorter only summarizes: the fullest Reformed treatment of the moral law, extended expositions of Christ's offices and the means of grace, and searching ethical application. The serious student of Reformed theology who stops at the Shorter has tasted only the introduction; the Larger Catechism is the fuller meal.
